specPoints.text: describe the effects of forces between bodies such as changes in speed, shape or direction
identify different types of force such as gravitational or electrostatic

primer.text: You already know that objects push and pull on one another. This note gathers those pushes and pulls into a single catalogue of named forces and then asks what any of them can actually do to the body it acts on. Two lessons follow: the catalogue of force types, then the effects a force can produce.

lessons.title: Naming the forces between interacting objects
sourceHeadings: What are the different types of forces?
lessons.opening: Whenever two objects interact, each one can push or pull the other, and physics gives that push or pull the name force. This lesson walks through the catalogue of everyday forces: weight, reaction, friction, drag, thrust, upthrust, electrostatic, magnetic and tension. For each entry, the key question is where the force comes from and which way it points.
keyPoints: A force is a push or a pull that arises whenever two objects interact.
A surface pushes back on anything resting on it; this reaction force acts at right angles to the surface.
Friction opposes the sliding of two surfaces, and drag is the same opposing action inside a fluid such as air or water.
Thrust is an engine-produced force that speeds an object up, while upthrust is the upward push a fluid exerts on a submerged body.
Charges and magnetic poles follow one pattern: like kinds repel, opposite kinds attract.
Tension acts along a rope or spring when its two ends are pulled apart.

low.restatement: Objects interact by pushing or pulling, and each named force on the list is one of those pushes or pulls. Resting surfaces push straight back; rubbing surfaces drag backwards.
low.analogy: Think of the catalogue like a class register: every force you will meet in this course has a name on it, and each name comes with the same two facts — what causes it and which way it acts.
low.examPointer: Naming questions are free marks if the definitions are exact: say 'reaction force acts perpendicular to the surface', not just 'the surface pushes'.

medium.restatement: Every entry in the catalogue is an interaction between two bodies: gravitational and electrostatic act at a distance, while reaction, friction, drag, thrust, upthrust and tension need contact or a medium.
medium.analogy: Sort the register into two boxes — 'needs to touch' and 'acts across space'. Weight and electrostatic fall in the second box; everything the surface or fluid does falls in the first.
medium.examPointer: Examiners penalise loose names: the gravitational force on an object is its weight (never bare 'gravity'), and air resistance is the air-specific case of drag.

check.stem: A football rests on horizontal grass. Which force does the grass exert on the ball, and how is it directed?

options.text: A downward gravitational pull towards the centre of the Earth
options.explanation: That pull is the Earth's weight force on the ball; the grass's own push points the other way.

options.text: A horizontal thrust force along the ground
options.explanation: Thrust is an engine-produced force; nothing in this scene supplies one.

options.text: A backward frictional force opposing motion
options.explanation: The ball is stationary, so nothing is sliding and no opposing frictional force is generated.

options.text: An upward push at right angles to the surface
options.explanation: A resting surface exerts a reaction force perpendicular to itself, here vertically upwards.

check.stem: A pebble sinks through a lake and steadily loses speed. Which interaction between pebble and water slows it?

options.text: Tension in the water pulling the pebble back
options.explanation: Tension needs a stretched rope or spring; a liquid cannot pull along a line like that.

options.text: Drag from the water flowing against its surface
options.explanation: Drag is the frictional action of a fluid; the water particles colliding with the pebble slow it down.

options.text: Upthrust alone, acting sideways
options.explanation: Upthrust acts vertically upward and does not by itself oppose the motion through the water.

options.text: Electrostatic attraction to the lake bed
options.explanation: No charged bodies are involved; the slowing needs a frictional mechanism.

check.stem: Two charged rods are brought close and each pushes the other away. What does this reveal about their charges?

options.text: They carry the same kind of charge, which repels
options.explanation: Like charges experience a repulsive push, so mutual pushing away signals like kinds.

options.text: They carry opposite charges, which repel
options.explanation: Opposite charges attract; repulsion is the like-charge behaviour.

options.text: One rod is uncharged and merely inert
options.explanation: An uncharged rod would not supply a mutual push; both are active here.

options.text: The charges have drained away
options.explanation: Drained charges would leave no force at all, not a push.

check.stem: The north poles of two magnets are brought towards each other. Each magnet experiences:

options.text: An attractive pull, because north seeks south
options.explanation: That rule pairs opposite poles; two north poles do not attract.

options.text: No force, because the poles are identical
options.explanation: Identical poles repel strongly; identical does not mean neutral.

options.text: A repulsive push, because like poles repel
options.explanation: The magnetic rule mirrors the electrostatic one: like kinds repel.

options.text: A force that alternates with distance
options.explanation: The force weakens with distance but keeps its repulsive direction here.

check.stem: Two children pull opposite ends of a rope towards themselves. Which force acts along the rope, and what does it do to each child?

options.text: Upthrust, lifting both children's hands
options.explanation: Upthrust belongs to fluids; no fluid acts here.

options.text: Tension, pulling back on each child's hands
options.explanation: Pulling the rope's ends apart puts the rope under tension, which pulls inward on each holder.

options.text: Drag, because the rope moves through air
options.explanation: The rope need not move at all for tension to exist; drag is irrelevant here.

options.text: Reaction from the ground, transmitted up the rope
options.explanation: The ground's reaction acts on feet, not along the rope's length.

check.stem: State, in your own words, what a force is.
check.modelAnswer: A force is a push or a pull that arises from the interaction between two objects.

check.stem: Name the upward push a liquid exerts on a submerged object.
check.modelAnswer: Upthrust — the upward-acting push the fluid exerts on anything fully or partly submerged in it.

check.stem: Explain why a heavy boat floating on a lake stays at the surface instead of sinking.
check.modelAnswer: The water pushes up on the hull with a force called upthrust. Where the boat floats, that upward push equals the boat's weight, so the two cancel and no resultant force remains to pull the boat under.

check.stem: A ball is pushed underwater and released. Name the force that makes it shoot upward and state its direction.
check.modelAnswer: Upthrust acts on the ball: the surrounding water exerts an upward-acting push, so the ball accelerates towards the surface.

lessons.title: What a force can change: speed, direction, shape
lessons.opening: The catalogue answers 'which force?', but not 'so what?'. This lesson closes that gap: whatever its name, a force acting on a body can change how fast it moves, which way it moves, or what shape it is. One diagram, three effects — and every mechanics question in this course hangs off one of them.
keyPoints: A force acting on a body can change that body's speed, its direction of travel, or its shape.
Thrust from an engine speeds a vehicle up, while braking friction slows it down.
A sideways gravitational pull, such as the Sun's on a comet, bends the direction of travel without contact.
Opposing pushes on the ends of a spring squash it — a change of shape.
Which effect appears depends on the type of force acting and how it is applied.

low.restatement: Every force on the catalogue list can do one or more of three jobs: make the body faster or slower, turn it, or deform it.
low.analogy: Three dials on a control panel: pace, heading, form. Any force turns at least one dial.
low.examPointer: When a question asks 'state the effect', answer with one of the three exact nouns: speed, direction, shape.

medium.restatement: The effect of a force is not fixed by the force's name alone: the same catalogue entry can act along the motion (speed change), across it (direction change) or against the body's form (shape change).
medium.analogy: One hand on a rolling ball can pat it forwards (faster), nudge its side (turning) or squeeze it (flattening) — the hand's role selects the dial.
medium.examPointer: Two-mark questions often want the pair 'effect + force name'; 'friction, which changes the speed' scores both, 'friction' alone scores one.

check.stem: A comet far from any solid body bends its path as it passes the Sun. Which effect of force does this show?

options.text: A change of shape of the comet
options.explanation: Nothing compresses or stretches the comet here; its route, not its form, changes.

options.text: A change of direction of travel
options.explanation: A sideways gravitational pull turns the path without any contact at all.

options.text: A change of the Sun's shape
options.explanation: The question asks about the comet, and the Sun's form is untouched.

options.text: No effect, because nothing touched the comet
options.explanation: Forces act at a distance too; contact is not required for an effect.

check.stem: A cyclist squeezes the brakes and slows down. Which force produces the change, and which effect is it?

options.text: Friction; a change of speed
options.explanation: Braking friction opposes the motion and reduces the speed — a change of speed.

options.text: Thrust; a change of speed
options.explanation: Thrust would speed the bicycle up; braking is the opposing action.

options.text: Tension; a change of direction
options.explanation: No rope acts here, and the route is straight — the speed changes.

options.text: Reaction; a change of shape
options.explanation: The wheel-surface reaction supports the rider; it is not the slowing mechanism.

check.stem: A spring is squeezed from both ends until it is shorter. Which force effect has been demonstrated?

options.text: Change of direction
options.explanation: The spring is not rerouted; its form changed.

options.text: Change of speed
options.explanation: The spring ends at rest; no speeding up is involved.

options.text: Change of shape
options.explanation: Opposing pushes at the ends deform the spring — the shape effect.

options.text: No effect, because the spring stayed in place
options.explanation: Staying in place says nothing about deformation; the shape clearly changed.

check.stem: An engine's thrust and the surrounding drag act on a plane in level flight, with the thrust larger. The plane will:

options.text: Slow down, because drag always wins
options.explanation: Drag only wins when it is larger; here the thrust exceeds it.

options.text: Hold a steady speed, because the forces are horizontal
options.explanation: Horizontal but unequal forces leave a resultant along the motion.

options.text: Speed up, because the resultant acts along the motion
options.explanation: With thrust ahead of drag, the surplus force changes the speed upward.

options.text: Change shape, because engines deform aircraft
options.explanation: Nothing here deforms the airframe; the motion's pace is what changes.

check.stem: Which list names exactly the three effects a force can have on a body?

options.text: Speed, direction, shape
options.explanation: These are the three effects of record: a force can change how fast, which way, or what form.

options.text: Speed, mass, temperature
options.explanation: Mass and temperature are not listed force effects.

options.text: Direction, colour, shape
options.explanation: Colour is not a mechanical effect of force.

options.text: Shape, weight, speed
options.explanation: Weight is itself a force, not an effect a force produces.

check.stem: List the three effects a force can have on a body.
check.modelAnswer: A force can change the body's speed, its direction of travel, or its shape.

check.stem: Name the force that speeds a vehicle up and the one that slows it under braking.
check.modelAnswer: Thrust from the engine speeds the vehicle up; braking friction slows it down.

check.stem: Explain why a comet's path bends even though nothing ever touches it.
check.modelAnswer: The Sun's gravitational pull is a force that acts across empty space. A force needs no contact: acting partly sideways to the comet's motion, that pull turns the travel direction, which is the direction effect.

check.stem: A tennis ball strikes a racket: at the instant of contact it squashes, then it departs on a new heading at a lower pace. Identify the force effects in order.
check.modelAnswer: During contact the ball's shape changes; leaving the strings its direction of travel is altered; and the reduced departure pace is the speed effect — all three force effects in one strike.

glossary.definition: A push or a pull that arises from the interaction between two objects.
The perpendicular push a surface exerts on an object resting on it.
The upward-acting push a fluid exerts on a fully or partly submerged object.
The frictional force a fluid exerts against an object moving through it.
The pulling force transmitted along a rope or spring when its ends are pulled apart.
